title: White Dwarfs Aren’t Just White. Scientists Discover Dying Stars Turning Pink and Green
gist: A study in RAS Techniques and Instruments finds that cool white dwarfs can look pink, purple, yellow, green or baby blue. The colors come from very dense atmospheres (about 1 g/cm³) and from debris of destroyed planets and asteroids. Of 152 white dwarfs within 65 light-years, five had unusual colors, about one in thirty, and the study suggests earlier surveys over-sampled hot, blue ones.

themes.theme: Atmospheric density drives white dwarf color

insights.claim: The atmospheres of the coolest white dwarfs can reach about 1 gram per cubic centimeter, roughly a million times denser than the sun's atmosphere. At that density, trace carbon, calcium and sodium interact with the dense helium plasma and absorb light across a wider range of colors.
insights.speaker: Petr Kubala
insights.so_what: Physics of dense plasma, not temperature alone, sets the visible color of these stellar remnants.
insights.quote: The researchers posit that density is the deciding factor.

themes.theme: Sampling bias in white dwarf surveys

insights.claim: Of 152 white dwarfs within 65 light-years of Earth, only five showed unusual coloration. That suggests roughly one in thirty white dwarfs shines with unusually colored light.
insights.speaker: Petr Kubala
insights.so_what: Most white dwarfs really are white, and colorful ones are a small minority.
insights.quote: Only five of them showed unusual coloration, suggesting that approximately one in thirty white dwarfs in the universe shines with unusually colored light.

insights.claim: The earlier belief that white dwarfs are mostly blue may come from sampling bias. The hottest ones are also the brightest and can be seen from farther away, so studies over-represent blue stars.
insights.speaker: Petr Kubala
insights.so_what: Surveys limited by brightness can skew how a population looks, a lesson that applies to observational datasets generally.
insights.quote: Because they’re easier to observe, many studies end up over-representing blue stars.
